consensus_summary: The dominant consensus identifies hell as the final state or realm of divine judgment and punishment for the unrepentant, commonly involving irreversible separation from God. It also recognizes, as a common lexical qualification or alternative, that English “hell” translates several distinct biblical terms.
book_summary: The book identifies “hell” not as one scriptural place or state but as an ambiguous English translation label. Each occurrence must be reclassified according to whether the underlying term is Sheol, Hades, Gehenna, or tartaroō/Tartarus.
consensus_core_identification: Hell is the final punitive destiny of the wicked after divine judgment.
book_core_identification: Hell is a many-to-one English translation label with no single biblical referent.
boundary_disagreement: The book rejects automatically grouping passages translated “hell” under one final-punishment referent. It reallocates Sheol and Hades passages to the realm of the dead, Gehenna passages to Gehenna/Valley of Hinnom, and tartaroō to Tartarus. Some Gehenna or Tartarus cases may still concern punitive judgment, so the extensions overlap without sharing the same organizing identification.
material_contradiction: The consensus treats “hell” primarily as a unified theological destination, whereas the book explicitly denies that the English word has a single scriptural referent. Accepting the book’s core therefore replaces the consensus’s doctrinal referent with a translation-label classification, even though the traditional doctrine remains acknowledged in the common-view note.
rationale: This is divergent rather than refined because the book does not merely narrow the duration, imagery, or occupants of the consensus hell; it changes what the term fundamentally identifies. It is not novel, since Responses A and C explicitly list the same Sheol/Hades/Gehenna/Tartarus distinction as a recognized scholarly reading.
strongest_objection: Showing that English “hell” translates multiple original-language terms does not by itself prove that those terms cannot contribute to a coherent theological category of final judgment. The printed references illustrate lexical diversity, but they do not alone establish all asserted meanings or exclude substantial conceptual overlap among the referents.
